subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Behind Motion No. 21 is the broader, philosophical approach to the whole question of Canadianization. Many people have asked what is the difference between the approach of the Conservative party on Canadianization and the approach of the Liberal party on Canadianization? As I said in my earlier remarks, when we were in government we accepted the 50 per cent objective of Canadianization in the oil and gas industry. I shall also remind members of this House that we made no attempts, contrary to what many members have said, prior to the 1979 election to weaken the operations of the Foreign Investment Review Agency. I was in cabinet and I had some involvement with the operations of the Foreign Investment Review Agency. During that time we were trying to improve the operations so that it would not be the stumbling block to investment, which has been the case since our time in government and was the case before our time in government. At no time were the operations and general intent of the Foreign Investment Review Agency undermined. I believe before and during our time in office the statistics show the operations were about the same.
We feel there is a positive way of achieving Canadianization and a negative way in achieving Canadianization. We have chosen the positive way. It involves greater encouragement to job creation and to investment in this country. It does not entail the very powerful negatives we have seen develop over the last few months.
Let me give a few clear indications, apart from the very clear differences under Bill C-48, how we would proceed on Canadianization. We would encourage Canadian ownership. The budget of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) would encourage Canadian ownership of companies through the Canadian stock investment plan. This plan would provide a shelter for Canadian investors against capital gains of Canadian-owned and controlled companies. We felt this would strongly encourage investment in Canadian companies, and would have a very positive effect on the Canadian ownership position in the Canadian oil and gas industry.
The proposal we put forward on Petro-Canada, a proposal that was made public shortly after the fall of our government in December of 1979, provided for a broad Canadian private sector involvement in that company. It also provided for Petro-Canada itself to go out, as part of its mandate, and buy a Canadian subsidiary of a multinational oil and gas company. We did not tell them they had to do that; we said that the new board of directors might find it was appropriate for the company to do it, and that they might find it was within their financial means to do it. We provided the financial means during the course of the proposal on Petro-Canada.
Another way we encouraged Canadian investment in this country was through two amendments on the treatment of

October 23, 1981

capital gains and on registered retirement savings plans. One of the amendments allowed farmers to take $100,000 of their capital gain on the sale of a farm, place it in an RRSP and use the RRSP funds to invest in the Canadian economy. This, again, would have provided a strong incentive to the acquisition of Canadian common shares.
The key approach we would follow would be to encourage Canadian ownership through incentives. We would use the private sector, both companies and individuals, to participate fully in this process.
In contrast, the Liberal approach has been a more negative approach. In Bill C-48 they impose their 25 per cent ownership, and not full compensation for that ownership, on projects that are under way. They would not take the risk that the private sector had taken in bringing the project to the exploration stage.
The Liberals have proposed a tightening of, and a greater intervention in, the activities of the Foreign Investment Review Agency. We do not know where that stands.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) has said that is still in the mill. Other sources have said that that proposal has been pulled back. We do not know where it stands. We do know, however, that the existence of those proposals is casting a cloud over future investment in this country.
I believe the government must say one way or the other where they stand on that issue. Until we have that proposal dealt with one way or the other, it is going to have a negative effect on investment in this country. If there is a negative effect on investment in this country, there is going to be a negative effect on job creation. When we have 8.2 per cent unemployment, 900,000 people unemployed in this country, and expectations are that the number will increase further as we go further into the winter, we should not be deterring investment and we should not be deterring the creation of jobs in this country. Finally, the Liberals have interposed a much greater degree of state involvement through the operations of Petro-Canada.
In my earlier remarks, I said that Petro-Canada was perfectly eligible to go out and buy the subsidiaries of non-resident oil and gas companies. What we saw in the acquisition of Petrofina was the sloppiest acquisition that I have seen in my 18 years of experience in the investment business. A year ago September the shares were trading at less than $60 a share. Somehow or other, rumours got out that Petro-Canada was going to buy Petrofina. So what happened during that period? We had periodic run-ups in the value of those shares to the point when at $90 per share they said, "Yes, we are going to buy this company." What price did they say they would pay for it? Not $90 per share but $120 per share, more than twice the value of the company when those rumours started to occur and when Petro-Canada started the negotiations with Petrofina. This is what I mean when I say it is the sloppiest operation I have seen in my experience in the investment business. That sloppiness has cost Canadians, through the increased amounts of money that have been sent out of the
Canada Oil and Gas Act
country to create jobs in Brussels, many valuable tax dollars which could have been much better spent in this country.

That is why we said in the approach that we put forward on Petro-Canada a couple of years ago that we wanted Petro-Canada governed by private sector disciplines so they would not waste the tax dollars of people in this country. They would have been more careful-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: You wanted to dismantle Petro-Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURES RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS

No, sir. I hear the old myth surfacing once again. The hon. member said that we wanted to dismantle Petro-Canada. That was back about five years ago, in the early stages of the development of Petro-Canada. The former minister of energy can set the hon. member straight on that. When we were in government, we said that we would help Petro-Canada to grow and to be a powerful, profitable, large company in the oil and gas industry. This is what the proposal we put forward was to do. It would have been a stronger and more effective company in the oil and gas industry. It would have done more to create oil and gas development than the company which is being run by the government at this point in time.
I should like to return to the point at issue which I was discussing before I was interrupted by the Groucho Marx opposite. The key of the Liberal approach is more government ownership and more government intervention in the economy. Basically, it is negative in its direction.
The approach put forward by the Progressive Conservative Party would have led to a more positive investment environment in Canada, to more job creation, to a stronger Canadian dollar and to less inflation. This is the key. If it leads to less inflation, it will lead to lower interest rates. There is not a man or a woman in the country who does not believe that we need lower interest rates. This is the approach we would take if we were in government today. Canadians are becoming more and more anxious to see the Conservative party on the government side of the House so that it can make decisions which will create jobs and reduce the onerous level of interest rates.
I want hon. members opposite to listen carefully to my remarks. The Liberal approach clearly results in a negative business climate. I do not think there is a man or a woman in business in the country today who would say that the business climate is good. Yesterday I had occasion to speak with a man who said that the business climate in Canada is the worst he

We will see who is all hot air. The government has weakened the economy through its proposals in Bill C-48 and its proposals on Canadianization. It is the cause of the problems today. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) blamed it on the Federal Reserve Bank, President Reagan, the gnomes of Zurich, and the international monetary community. The problems today are being caused by the government. Hon. members opposite on the back benches should get after the members on the front benches. Perhaps they do not want to do it in Parliament because they would not want to be seen attacking the government. I hope they are doing this in the privacy of their caucus, because the country requires some independent thinking. We are not getting it from the Minister of Finance. There is great cost to the approach of the government on Canadianization, both through Bill C-48 and its other measures.
It makes me sick to hear the hypocrisy of the New Democratic Party. Time and again members of that party say that we must reduce interest rates. They demand that interest rates be dropped. At the same time they propose policies which will force investment money and jobs out of the country into other countries of the world and will force up interest rates. This is totally inconsistent and irresponsible.

It pushes the government to increase the impact of these policies. What is happening to the relationship between Canada and the United States? This relationship is being severely damaged. The other night I commented on the fact that the relationship between Canada and the United States is at its worst level since 1812. The reason I made that statement was that many times over the past years we have been concerned because the United States has not paid too much attention to us and has ignored the fact that we are up here. The United States is taking action with regard to its problems on the worldwide basis. This has a negative impact upon us, which the Americans do not understand. The United States has been passive, but it is the First time I have even seen a United States government threatening to take active, aggressive action against Canada in retaliation for the problems created by our government.
We cannot afford to ignore our largest neighbour and trading partner when it starts thinking that way. The government is, in fact, ignoring and provoking the United States. Hon. members of the government, such as the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien), went to the United States and made provocative statements, which encouraged the retaliatory action which is being proposed down there. I wonder why the government wants to provoke the United States Congress? Does it want to create an outside enemy to deflect attention from the problems in the country? I am less concerned about the actual actions taken by the administration or the United States Congress. I am more concerned about the signals this will send out to many people in the United States who have interests in one form or another in Canada and to individuals in Canada who may decide to move money outside the country. This is what concerns me most. It happened earlier this year, and the government has shown no intention of reversing its decision.
As I said, this has had a very important effect on the high interest rates that resulted from protecting the outflow of capital. That is the problem we have to fight. But there is

another way, a positive way of using the private sector, Mr. Speaker. It is a much more efficient way than using government. We would encourage development, we would encourage investment, and we would encourage the creation of jobs at a time when that is so important.
Which way should we be going? I ask members on the government side to tell me why the approach proposed in Motion No. 21 cannot be considered. It is a more positive approach to Canadianization than the negative approach that the government has taken.

There is a very clear and specific provision in Motion No. 21, and I hope the hon. member opposite will speak to it. I ask hon. members opposite to tell us why they think this motion is not appropriate. I asked the minister, and he said that we have a difference of opinion on it. I have given him my reasons why I think the approach taken in Bill C-48 is not appropriate, so I think I am entitled to expect that hon. members opposite will tell me why they think Motion No. 21 is not appropriate.
Members on the government side and in the NDP have said that Norway does this. Norway is not Canada, Mr. Speaker; it is a country that consumes about 15 per cent or 20 per cent of its oil and gas reserves. We in Canada import 15 per cent or 20 per cent, while Norway exports about 80 per cent of its oil. It can afford to take a different position and to risk that the private sector will cut back its involvement in the industry. Norway can afford to turn off development and take more aggressive attitudes than we can. We cannot afford to take that position. We need the oil.
If the government were serious about the objectives of self-sufficiency in oil, it would not bring Bill C-48 forward in its present form.
That is the basis for Motion No. 21, Mr. Speaker, I hope we will receive an adequate response from hon. members opposite.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to discuss this very important motion, Motion No. 21, and to connect it with Motion No. 22. The motion is concerned with the development of our resources to the maximum, in the most efficient manner, and with the least amount of intrusion by government.
Without these amendments, the government will continue to govern in an inequitable way. One industry will be singled out for unfair treatment.
Essentially what we have to deal with is the theft, by confiscation, of 25 per cent of northern lands, irrespective of who did the initial development and exploration work. No matter what private company, Canadian or international, did the work, by writing a regulation, the government has established that it can claim 25 per cent of whatever is produced without paying any compensation. No other industry in

Canada is subject to such harassment by the federal government.
I cannot help but believe that this is a reflection of the bias of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). It shows his disdain for western Canada, a disdain which is reiterated in his speeches and his personal attacks on the regions of Canada.

An hon. member opposite says "sick". I would like to share with him something that I believe to be far worse. Just two nights ago, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources spoke in Sherbrooke, Quebec. A report of that speech reads as follows:
Lalonde said a stronger threat to Canadian unity than Quebec nationalism could soon be posed by the growing wealth of Alberta.
Canada, he said, could one day become a country with one rich province imposing its whims on the other nine if Alberta uses its billions to take control of foreign companies and the federal government does not maintain its role of enforcing the sharing of wealth between rich and poor provinces.
The other nine provinces would eventually be at the mercy of Alberta's every fancy, he said, and a wave of (Alberta) nationalism of unprecedented strength could rise up if the federal government held back now from showing its teeth. "We don't pay enough attention to this threat" Lalonde said, "but it's a real one, it's there."
I submit that it is wrong to pick out one province and say that it is a threat to national unity. It suggests that that province is not willing to share. It flies in the face of everything that has been talked about with regard to the Constitution in the last 15 months. Federalism cannot work when the major player, the federal government, singles out one region and tries to draw the anger of the rest of the country against it.
The fact is that Alberta has a product that is worth world price, and it has negotiated with the federal government to sell that product at 75 per cent of its value within the next five years. To date, Alberta has contributed $30 billion to confederation by selling its product at less than world price. I submit that no other region in Canada can make such a claim.
The government claims that it will Canadianize the oil industry. This industry is located essentially in one region of Canada and that is not central Canada. When the government uses the term "Canadianize", it twists the language. It is really referring to a program of nationalization. This proposal was made in the same year that the government gave a guaranteed loan of $240 million to Chrysler Corporation and in the same year that it took Massey-Ferguson close to its breast to help it out. The unique difference between these multinational companies is that Massey-Ferguson and Chrysler are located in central Canada, while the oil industry is located away from the centre.
The people across this land do not mind the objective stated in the new energy program if it means a greater degree of Canadianization; but we do not have Canadianization, we have nationalization. We have nationalization of that industry which is located away from the centre. It was very much

reflected in the speech which was made the day before yesterday by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources when he was speaking of the province of Alberta. He said that we do not pay enough attention to that threat, but it is a real one and it is there. It shows the mentality of those who are now governing that they believe not in federalism or in a united Canadian family, but, rather, in a situation where they have power and control. They keep hoisting up the words, multinational oil companies, multinational oil companies, multinational oil companies", as if they wanted one to believe that those were evil words which would somehow produce the same kind of reaction as might appear on the face of a ten-year-old when he is told to clean out the bird cage. They believe the "multinational oil companies" are bad words.
The people of western Canada want to ask what it is that is so awful about our multinational oil companies that the federal government needs to come in and confiscate 25 per cent under the titles called Canada lands, and what it is that makes the government want to take over multinational oil companies and run them as it runs post offices and other institutions. However, when the multinational is Chrysler Corporation or Massey-Ferguson, the government is out there licking off the dollar bills and handing them out, hoping they can save this good company.
If we want to have a greater degree of Canadianization, so be it. Let us take a look at Canadian industries and multinational industries and set up a program. However, any time the government starts to be selective, choosing one industry which affects one region and then virtually promising in the House of Commons that it will not touch any other industry, that this program will not apply to any other industry, then its program of selectivity is one that is foul and wrong-

speechtext:
-and ought to be resisted by every Canadian.
I see the parliamentary secretary wincing at that. He has been wincing long enough, with many of our oil rigs leaving and having left the country, heading for Denver, for Australia, for Oklahoma, for Texas, and all of the other various oil centres in North America.
When we talk about the vast number of oil rigs which have left because of this program, those of us who represent western constituencies, believe that when we talk about a rig leaving, everyone understands it as well as we do. Throughout this past year, I became conscious of the past that when we say a rig is leaving, most people outside of the oil producing regions do not really understand what we are saying. I believe they imagine that there is a truck with a derrick on it heading out of the country, that we have lost a truck, an associate driver, and something called a derrick which is being pulled behind. The fact is that when one loses a rig, involved in the move are about 16 liner trucks loaded with batteries of equipment and tools, compressor stations, extra power plants and the rig itself. The total cost of moving a single rig is in the neighbourhood of half a million dollars, nearly $500,000. Far more than 100 of those rigs, with all the men and equipment that go with them,
have been driven out of the oil-producing parts of western Canada. They are heading off to the United States to drill wells and generate jobs there. Why? It is all in the name of some government in disguise which says that it is going to produce great national security and energy.
These Liberals on the other side have no representation in western Canada, with the exception of two members from Winnipeg. Perhaps it would be fair for me to remind them that when the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) first came to power, there were 56 elected Liberals west of the Manitoba border. Now there are three: two in the federal government, and one in the Manitoba legislature. That is what their policies have done to their respectability as viewed in the west. The fact is that they all had this notion that somehow they would tell Canadians that they were going to Canadianize, using all of those words that the Gallup polls told them to be pleasing. The truth is that they have considerably lowered our potential to produce oil and they have greatly reduced our possibilities for self-sufficiency by 1990.
Oh, how I wish there could have been a number of those Liberals with me when I saw some of these hard-working, private, Canadian business people at the auctions this past year, selling off their equipment because they had gone bankrupt. Oh, what a message they would have received! I know the risks that some of those young fellows took, having grown up on farms, having bought trucks, drilling rigs, and compressors, working virtually 24 hours a day, day after day, through Saturdays and Sundays, finally getting little fleets of five or six trucks going. There they were, somewhere in the middle of their lives, having everything auctioned off.
With the lack of confidence in the new energy program, what did we have? We had a sale taking place where one could hardly get a bid. Relatively new oil equipment was being sold for virtually the same kind of prices at which one could buy older farm trucks. It was a crying shame. There was certainly no need for this at all.
What we have is a situation where the government has given itself the power to come in and claim 25 per cent of all discoveries of oil on lands north of 60, irrespective of who does the work and the exploration or makes the discovery. Moreover, irrespective of what company does the development, the federal government can come in and give a licence to its own chief agency, PetroCan. I submit that all of that will do nothing other than cause a tremendous depression in the development of our high north.
I know that many people hold the view that our energy future is secure because of the fact that we will always be able to find some more oil. I believe that we have the potential for security for a great length of time into the future. We have a 300-year supply of oil at least which is extracted by way of the compression of coal, forcing it by liquefaction into oil. We have a tremendous potential in our tar sands and we also have a great potential that is yet untapped. However, what is not realized, and what the Canadian people are not fully aware of is that the oil of tomorrow will not be nearly as cheap as the oil of today. Those who do not know the industry, believe that
October 23, 1981

somehow the way one finds oil is to hunt around, drill a hole, and that a lake of it lies underground. They believe that once one has found that pool, put the pipe down and put the pump on, the price of oil should be the same from the day one discovers it, allowing for inflation, until the pool is dry. That is not the situation.
Oil is found underground in a tertiary formation. It is in a sandstone rock, similar to one's bathroom sponge. The newspapers or the media describe the first oil which was discovered in western Canada, the Turner Valleys or the Leducs, as blowouts, gushers or high pressure wells from which oil shoots up several hundred feet into the air. There was oil all over the derricks, the men and the vehicles around. It was very cheap then because once the pool was discovered, the pressure of the oil forced the weight of the formations of the earth to shoot that oil up into the air. The pressure of the oil just pumped it horizontally to the refinery. That lasted for perhaps as long as ten years. Then, approximately five or six years ago, along came the rocking donkey head pumps. We then went into the period during which hot salt water known as brine was pumped down into the formations. That is the stage at which most of our oil wells are today. Those of us near the oil industry use a term all too loosely, I submit, when we say we will be out of oil in eight years' time. What we are really saying is that we will be out of the present methods of extracting the oil by that time. The truth of the matter is that when we say we will be out of oil eight years from today, there will still be 75 per cent of the original finds in the tertiary formation. It will not be in the big holes in the tertiary formation, it will be confined to little, minuscule holes, and new methods of getting the large volume of oil out will be required. This is what is generally referred to as enhanced recovery. You have to use a solvent such as Varsol, or some kind of solvent, to loosen it up and get it to flow. All of our future oil will come from enhanced recovery offshore, from the north slopes, from the tar sands or in situ. Every one of those shows a sharp upswing on the chart in terms of cost. Any of the clauses in the present legislation that discourages incentives will cause a dramatic downward pressure on our ability to develop a find, because the costs are going to rise sharply as we move rapidly out of the period during which we have enjoyed free running oil into a period when we will have developed or enhanced oil through the use of some solution, or else we will have to explore many more distant regions, which will not allow for the kind of development we would all like to see.
With regard to the whole question of Canadianization, the government, knowing that Canadians like the word "Canadi-anize" and do not really like the word "multinational", uses these words selectively, with the feeling that somehow they must obtain control of the industry. If it is a question of ownership generally across the industry, industry has already indicated the degree to which it would favour such a position. If it is to be selective ownership, we wonder what the motives of the government are.
Canada Oil and Gas Act
More important, Sir, the government does not need the kind of control it speaks of. Today the government controls the industry as it did last year, the year before and five years before that, in so far as drilling is concerned, where you drill, when you drill, when you bring a well or field into production, also in so far as all the environmental controls are concerned, where the pipelines will go, who will build them, and what strengths of steel are to be used. It also controls refining, the quality and the amount to be sold on the export and on the domestic markets. This is all done through the National Energy Board and through the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. All the necessary controls are there, and if they are not, they can easily be put into place.
It is not necessary for government to own the industry and at the same time to write the rules with respect to that industry. What we have today is quite literally a case where the referee is one of the players in the game. In those lands north of 60, the federal government is fully knowledgeable about every formation and hole that has been drilled by an oil company. This information is all banked in the National Energy Board's closet, or library. It is fully aware of all that information. It owns an oil company and is able to compete. When any company, be it Ranger Oil, or whatever it might be, puts down a hole-and most often those exploration holes are drilled by wholly Canadian-owned companies-a full profile of the hole-whether it is dry or otherwise, whether there is gas or oil below, the kind of formations that are encountered-is mapped and sent to the National Energy Board, so the government has a complete map of all Canada's drillings.
The same minister who is in charge of all that information is also in charge of the energy company, namely, Petro-Canada. I submit that the way this game is played is simply not fair. One company has access to all the information, and on that basis an inequity exists. In view of the existence of that inequity, I think it is important that we accept the proposed changes in the amendment in Motion No. 21 in order to eliminate this situation of inequity, which is obvious, especially north of 60.

Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 21 contains a very important element of Bill C-48 which we are addressing today. I want to read it just to emphasize how important the subject is. It states:
Her Majesty in Right of Canada is hereby vested with and the Minister on her behalf shall hold a share sufficient to render the interest holder with a Canadian ownership rate of fifty per cent.
The key words in that, of course, are "a share sufficient to render the interest holder with a Canadian ownership rate of fifty per cent".
This motion really addresses what we consider a very fundamental part of Bill C-48, a very fundamental and significant element of this particular bill. The subject of Canadianization is a subject that I think intrigues all members of this House and all people in Canada. As a result, during the committee stage of this bill a great deal of time was spent discussing this particular issue, the implications of it and the possible roots of implementation.

October 23, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
Essentially, the question is: what does Canadianization mean? To my way of thinking, it means we have a Canadian corporation involved in the development of oil or gas, we have Canadian capital being used for that development, and we have Canadian jobs. In other words, Canadian people are the ones involved in the development of this particular product in the north, with Canadian people being given the opportunity to earn those incomes and gain their livelihood in this way. I do not believe anybody questions that or doubts the importance or relevance of it.
The concern arises from what we effectively have in Bill C-48 as it now stands. Do we really have Canadianization? My concern is that we are getting involved here in something called "double speak". We call it Canadianization, but in fact what we have is nationalization. The reason for that is very simple. When I talked about Canadianization, I was talking about Canadian companies, Canadian content, Canadian capital and Canadian jobs. That is what we are after. There is no need to make any further change. That is the goal we have and that is what we want to accomplish.
As Bill C-48 stands at the moment, the government is not content to take over 25 per cent ownership of a U.S. company out of the United States or 25 per cent of a European company. It is more concerned with what it is in fact doing, that is, taking over 25 per cent of Canadian companies. I begin to wonder right away how that could possibly be called Canadianization. Surely there is a confusion of terms. What we will actually and effectively end up with is nationalization, and nationalization is the fundamental principle we should be discussing and considering very carefully.
When I spoke on Bill C-48 in the past, I said it is a fundamental and important bill. It is the start of a whole lot of future activity in the north, and it is the start of an opportunity for many people in that part of the country who up until now have not had access to some of these jobs. Very often they are faced with high unemployment and with very few options from which to choose.
I think it is fairly commonly accepted that if you want to accomplish something that is difficult or something to which there may not be immediate acceptance in the arena of politics, the popular thing to do, something that is done very regularly, is to create what we call a straw man, an enemy. Often that enemy is not a real enemy but a figure of speech or somewhat of an illusion. I think that is what we are involved with right here, the creation of a straw man. The government's purported goal is Canadianization, but it creates a straw man by saying everything is owned by multinationals and foreigners. It is a laudable goal. Why would the government turn around and take 25 per cent of the Canadian corporations? If we look carefully, we can see that what it is really after is not Canadian content in industry, it is not Canadian content in opportunity, it is not Canadian content in capital but a real grab at control. Its justification for this is twofold. The first one is its need for a window on the industry. It has to see what is happening in the oilfields, what is happening to development
in the north. The second one is to have some control in the direction of that development.
I think that what we are ending up with and what is the real purpose behind Bill C-48 is nothing more than control of the industry. If the government really wanted Canadianization, it would leave Canadian companies alone. It would not take 25 per cent of their interests in their lands.
What concerns me most, Mr. Speaker, is that if the government can apply this philosophy, this straw man approach to this industry, why should it not do the same to other industries in our country?
Canada is involved in many industries. Look at the forest industry, for example. Anyone who has anything to do with the federal government knows the importance of the forest industry, otherwise we would not have all these papers. Canadian people have an interest in the forest industry, so why not apply the same philosophy there? Why not take 25 per cent of that industry, if the government's argument is valid?
How about the newspaper industry? I am sure the government has quite an interest in that industry because I am sure that quite often there are comments in the newspapers about members of the government that they would rather not see. Why not apply the same philosophy there?
Why not do the same in agriculture? Surely we have an interest in food production in our country. Why not apply the same philosophy in this industry? The fact is that we are not talking about Canadianization, Mr. Speaker; we are talking about control of an industry and its direction.
If the government were really interested in Canadianization, it would accept the motion brought forward by my hon. friend, the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) because it does address the matter. It calls for 50 per cent ownership. It calls for 50 per cent control. Therefore, that motion should be acceptable.
We can see, after discussing Bill C-48 over the last few days, the dangers incorporated in it. These dangers cause me great concern because of the effects it may have in the north for a long time to come. We have talked about ministerial discretion. We are talking about nationalization today under the guise of Canadianization. The government has demonstrated a real ignorance of what is happening in the north and has turned a deaf ear to the concerns those people have about Bill C-48. In fact, we did not even go up into the north.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE GROWTH OF RESERVE FORCE
speechtext:
that Bill C-359, to encourage the growth of the reserve force of the Canadian Forces, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased indeed to have the opportunity to speak on my bill C-359, an act to encourage the growth of the reserve force of the Canadian Forces. The explanation of the bill is indicated in the explanatory note as follows:
The purpose of this bill is to encourage support for the reserve force of the Canadian Forces.
What I am suggesting is that reservists must be given the opportunity to train without prejudice to their full-time employment. They must be given this opportunity without fear of reprisal from their employers, without sacrificing their regular vacation and without sacrificing their seniority.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, reserve force training usually takes place in the evenings and on weekends during the year. However, the culmination of such training and an exercise to which all members look forward is the annual training exercise of two weeks' duration when the reserve unit is brought together at a specified military centre.
Too frequently reserve force members, in particular the younger members, are unable to participate in such exercises because their employer cannot or will not provide leave for this
National Defence
purpose. Many young citizen soldiers do not have enough seniority in their employment to choose their holidays at the exact time of the reserve force training exercise to which their unit is directed. I remember taking these training exercises, but I was self-employed and did not have the same problem that many of these people have with their employer. Furthermore, some members are married and have a responsibility and natural inclination to spend a holiday period with their families.
At a time when the defence of one's country is very much an issue and when we as Canadians should get as much from our defence dollar as possible, a larger and better prepared reserve force is a desirable objective.
Military experts today talk of limited warfare engagements, with the major battleground taking place in Europe or the Middle East. Gone will be the opportunity of producing fighting men for it will be a "come as you are" battle. There will not be the time, as there was in the Second World War, when men went through their training and then on to battle.
I recall my own training. At the end of the war, I was still training in the RCAF. I received my wings after the war was over. It took over a-year of training before I was qualified. We certainly will not be able to wait that period of time if another war should develop. Hence, there is a need for a better prepared and equipped reserve to bolster the fighting force if a war should break out.
Canada has an unparalleled record when it comes to the willingness and the ability to fight and defend, not only its country but also those of our allies in times of war. The success of the Canadian Armed Forces has been credited to the higher degree of readiness and training that they have received.
Canada's reserve force consists of the primary reserve and the supplementary reserve. The supplementary reserve is a list of personnel, either retired or honourably released from the regular force, who have elected voluntarily to have their names remain on the list. As long as they meet age, medical requirements, and remain current in their trade or occupation, they are liable to call-out when the need arises.
When the Korean war broke out, I was called out for a period of four months to train recruits at the Royal Canadian Army Service Corps school at Camp Borden to fight in Korea. I did not get there myself, but many of those I trained were in the Korean war.
The primary reserve is made up of four components; the naval reserve, the milita or the reserve land force, the air reserve and the communication command reserve.
Let us look at the situation in 1945. Canada had a population of 12 million and a reserve of 83,264. Six years later, with a population increase of two million to 14 million, the number in the reserve had dropped by 30,000 to 53,525. Seven years later, when Canada had a population of 17 million, we had dropped slightly more but still had roughly the same number. In those seven years, our reserve force had not increased although our population had increased by three million. By 1971, with a population of 21 million, the reserve force had
12144

October 23, 1981
National Defence
decreased to 21,869. Last year, in 1980, with a population of 24 million, there were 20,265 serving in our reserve, less than one tenth of 1 per cent of our total population. It can be seen from the statistics that although our population increased over the years, the numbers in our reserve force have been decreasing dramatically. In the past, the reserves have been an integral and imperative part of the Canadian Armed Forces and served as the training ground and back-up force to the regular forces.
Today the role of the reserve is twofold. First, to enhance the war deterrence of the Canadian Armed Forces and, second, to support the regular force in ongoing peacetime tasks and activities. General Richard Rohmer, a retired chief of the reserve forces, said:
The role of the reserves force is to augment the regular force in times of peace, emergency or war.
Brigadier General Cowan, when testifying before the Senate Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs, revealed the extent of their role within the Armed Forces. He stated that it is the policy of the Department of National Defence that the regular forces and the reserve force be partners in the Canadian Armed Forces total force concept.
Historically, the reserve forces have always made a significant contribution to the total strenght of Canada's Armed Forces, and have played an important role in many military endeavours in both peace and war.
The reserves provide trained officers and men for reinforcement and they have a particularly important role in internal security contingency plans. First, the naval reserve maintains a control of shipping organizations for operation and expansion in time of emergency. Second, the militia also provides trained personnel for augmenting civil emergency operations, and third, the air reserve provides light tactical air transport.
Members of the reserve have always shown a great willingness to undergo training in peacetime to prepare themselves for active duty when called upon. Because their willingness is there, we need to provide a better arrangement for the reservists so that they may participate in training and educational activities provided by the armed services.
My bill pertains primarily to the public service and Crown corporations. As hon. members know, public servants in Canada come under the Financial Administration Act. Under military leave, section 47 reads:
A deputy head may grant to an employee leave of absence without pay for a period not exceeding three years for service in
(a)	the regular forces; or
(b)	the active service forces.
Section 48 states that a deputy head may grant leave of absence to an employee who is a member of the reserve forces for any period during which the employee is required to take annual training, attend parades, assist in disaster relief, and so on. This kind of training can be with or without pay.
I remember the floods in Toronto in the fifties. My regiment, the Irish Regiment of Canada, was called out to do duty at that time because of a natural disaster. I recall also the
Mississauga derailment disaster of not too long ago when some of the forces could have been called out. They could have carried on a very heavy role had they been required to do so.
The point I want to emphasize is that the deputy head may grant leave of absence. It is not demanded that he do so, but he may do so if he wishes. In effect, the government has encouraged employers, both in the private and in the public sector, to grant leave of absence to the reservists through a voluntary approach.
I believe the federal government should now implement legislation that will make it mandatory for leave of absence to be granted, both in the public sector and to employees of Crown corporations.
In 1978, the then Minister of National Defence, Mr. Barney Danson, set up the National Employers' Support Committee, called NESC. The members of this committee are prominent individuals in the business community. The committee encourages companies in the private sector to give reservists two weeks off in the summer to take their training, but it assures the employer that the employee will not lose job progression and the two weeks will not be considered as his vacation. The committee has been highly successful in the last three years. It appears that once executives in the business community are made aware of this need, most companies willingly grant the leave for reservist training.
The problems that NESC face are usually with the smaller companies. For example, if a company only has 20 employees and four of them want to go on reserve training at the same time this may create a real problem. However, this is the kind of situation that may be worked out. Certainly it may be a problem for the small-business man, but for companies such as General Motors and others, this should not be a real problem, and certainly not in the public sector or for Crown corporations.
As I said at the outset, I propose in this bill that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) encourage that similar leave be granted outside the federal public sector, and to this end I suggest that he enter into arrangements with employers in both the private and provincial sector.
The issue of pay and pay supplements to reservists when on leave of absence is an issue that the NESC leaves up to the employer and employee to work out between themselves. The National Employment Support Committee does not involve itself in that issue.
In the United States, legislation does exist that gives reserves and national guardsmen leave without loss in pay or time. Section 6323 of the United States Code dealing with military leave, reserves and national guardsmen, states:
An employee as defined by Section 2105 of this title or an individual employed by the government of the District of Columbia, permanent or temporary indefinite, is entitled to leave without loss in pay, time or performance or efficiency rating for each day, not in excess of 15 days in a calendar year in which he is on active duty or is engaged in field or coast defence training-
October 23, 1981

It also provides-and I think there is an amendment-that the number of days can be cumulative, so that if you do not use up the 15 days in one year, you may use up the days in the following year.
During the 1950s and 1960s in Canada, the reserve force was investigated at various times by a committee, a commission, a study and a departmental review. Implementation of many of the recommendations of these investigative bodies dramatically changed the role, the size and the structure of the reserve.
In May, 1953, the Chief of the General Staff established a committee under the chairmanship of Major General Howard Kennedy to examine the organization, training and administration of the reserve army and make recommendations on ways of improving its effectiveness. One of the most important recommendations made by the Kennedy committee was in response to the weakened state of the reserve force which was attributed, in the committee's opinion, to apathy on the part of the public. I certainly hope that is not the situation at the present time.
In their report, they stated:
.. . that the reserve forces are not only necessary but vital to the defence of Canada and deserve the support of all citizens.
I might point out that at that time the reserves were at a level of 53,000; whereas today they are less than 19,000.
In February of 1964, the Minister of National Defence approved the formation of the Suttie Commission, placed under the chairmanship of Brigadier General E. R. Suttie from whom it gained its name. As the Kennedy committee before it, the Suttie committee stressed the need for public support for the militia. It asked for a vigorous public relations campaign to be spearheaded by vocal government support at all levels; but this was not forthcoming.
The organizational changes resulting from the Suttie commission's recommendations were sweeping and structurally disruptive. They brought about a diminution in the strength of the reserve in terms of units and personnel and reduced its capability to recruit, train and to administer itself. Many units were "mothballed", including the regiment that I was part of at that time, the Irish Regiment of Canada.
I will conclude my comments soon, Mr. Speaker, if I may have your indulgence for a few more minutes.
In mid-1965, the establishment of an organization known as the Deputy Chief Reserves was approved by the Defence Council. From this review of the reserves evolved one of the most detailed and comprehensive tasking plan ever developed in peacetime.
Briefly, the militia was divided into three categories: First, the ready reserve which consisted of individuals trained to such a degree in their particular trade that they can fill in for the regular force; second, the regional reserve, composed of units and individuals required to reinforce other units and committed to the defence of Canada; and third, the mobile command reserve, consisting of those units that would form the training
National Defence
organization needed in an emergency to reinforce the regular force.
The creation of these categories led to a fundamental change in the reserve's system of training. No longer would units proceed to summer training camps as organized entities under their own commanding officers. In future, only subunits that were part of the mobile command reserve would proceed to summer camp, where they were grouped into units of battalion size for training under regular force commanders. Training for the balance of the reserve would be conducted at local unit headquarters at regular force schools and on job training with units and organizations requiring their support in the event of an emergency. In this way, it was felt that the training resources could be concentrated upon the tasks to be peformed, rather than a general and not too extensive training of all the militia for all foreseeable tasks.
The idea was efficient from a financial point of view, but it overlooked two vital areas: first, the training of senior militia officers in the handling of their own units and men; second, the development of that "esprit de corps" so necessary for holding a unit together, particularly under trying circumstances. It can only be developed through long periods of working and training together as an organized unit.
On March 24, 1981, a subcommittee of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence was formed. The subcommittee was empowered to study the status, capability and role of the Armed Forces Reserves and report to the committee not later than December 7, 1981.
I look forward to the tendering of this report to the Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. I hope my bill will have some impact on their findings and on the report.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, it is obvious from the bill I am proposing that it is to encourage support for the reserve force of the Canadian Forces. It does not go all the way but is, I submit, a step in the right direction toward making it easier for those in the public service and Crown corporations to serve in the reserves, and to encourage the private sector and the provincial public sector to do likewise, in the interest of all Canadians.

speechtext:
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson), who has had a distinguished military career, on bringing this matter to the attention of the House. I wish that members on that side would not write out a 40-minute speech and try to get through them in 20 minutes. I found it very difficult to understand what the hon. member was saying. However, I promise to read his speech in Hansard and find out exactly how much sense it made.
We are pleased that at least one person on that side of the House spoke about the interest in the defence of Canada. Usually, we do not hear anyone on that side speaking about the Armed Forces, unless it is to advise us of yet more reductions that are to take place, or when they speak on their favourite subject of the unification of the three armed services.

October 23, 1981
National Defence
The general intent of this bill is something that we, on this side, have no difficulty in supporting! During our brief term in office, when the Elon. Allan McKinnon was Minister of National Defence, we were setting up plans to support and expand the reserve forces. Unfortunately, we were not able to carry these out in any detail. This afternoon we have been given the information by the hon. member for Etobicoke-Lake-shore that since the government changed, there has been yet another reduction of, about 1,000 people in the Canadian reserves.
1 find it difficult to understand why we are dealing with this bill this afternoon in one way, and that is because the subject matter of this bill is already before the subcommittee of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence. This illustrates the confusion opposite when it comes to defence matters. Perhaps the hon. member did not know that that was the case.
I am interested in what will happen in the debate this afternoon, whether hon. members opposite will talk out their own bill or try to refer this matter to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence for further study. The committee already has a mandate to study it. I do not know what type of disposition hon. members opposite would like to make. I will watch very carefully.
I have referred to confusion in defence matters. 1 should like to add to that by indicating confusion and neglect in another area. 1 have the report of the Standing Senate Committee on Health, Welfare and Science entitled, "They Served-We Care". Recommendation No. 4 of the report reads as follows:
We recommend that all necessary steps be taken immediately to eliminate the unacceptable delays in processing pension applications and in pension adjudications which have accumulated since 1970-
Although there are some people like the hon. member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore who would like to see the government act, this illustrates that the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell) will just not act. The trouble in the administration of pensions has been brought to the attention of the House on many occasions. I hope this renewed interest will see the matter finally resolved.
There is some difficulty with the mechanism proposed by the hon. member in his bill, although we fully support the intent. If a number of employees in a particular branch of the public service all wanted to take leaves of absence at one time, it might adversely affect the operation of the department. One example which jumps to mind immediately is the post office. Another one would be the Northern Transportation Company Ltd., a Crown corporation. Its main business is done during the summer icefree season, a matter of two or three months. If at that time employees of that organization decided they wanted to take leave of absence, it would disrupt the very necessary service rendered. There might be some difficulty there. I was not sure whether the hon. member who made this proposal was thinking that leave of absence with pay should be
granted in all cases. If that were to be the case, it might be very expensive for the government.
I am pleased to see the hon. member indicating that he does not think that is necessary. Many people who serve in the reserve do not do it with a pecuniary interest. They do it to serve their country. I am pleased the hon. member takes that view also. If this were extended to private industry, the disruptive effects might be even greater.
The wording of Clause No. 2(2) of the proposed bill does not make sense. It is not a matter of law. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) may encourage someone to do something. He does not need legislative authority to encourage people to do things. He can do that as a matter of course. It is just an administrative matter. There is some difficulty with the way in which the bill is worded. Many of the items proposed in the bill could already be done by administrative arrangements. It is not necessary to introduce a new law into the statute books.
I am about to commit the same parliamentary error as the hon. member who spoke first. I will speak very briefly to the intent of the bill, which we have said we fully support, and then I will speak in general about the Canadian Armed Forces Reserve. This subject seldom comes before the House and I think it is worthy of some discussion.
The hon. member referred to the supplementary reserves, those who have served honourably in the regular forces and continue voluntarily to play a very valuable role. I thought the primary reserve consisted of 20,000 people, but I have been informed that it now consists of 19,000 people and is shrinking every day. As the hon. member said, it is divided into four main sections, the first one being the militia, the oldest section having beein established in 1855. In the 1870s at the time of the Fenian raids, some 40,000 men served in the Canadian militia. At the time of those troubles, or of potential troubles between British North America and the United States of America, the main defence force in Canada consisted of the militia. They kept Canada safe from becoming part of what is now the United States, if we look at it that way. Then we have the naval reserve and the air reserve. It was very interesting to see just a few days ago the last flight of the single Otter in the Canadian Air Reserve. These have been replaced by Kiowa helicopters. The single Otter has been retired after a number of years of honourable service with the Canadian Air Reserve. Also there is the communications reserve. It is a very small unit consisting of 1,500 or so people.

speechtext: What about the rangers?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE GROWTH OF RESERVE FORCE
speechtext:
They have a special place in my heart. I will speak about them in a moment.
The reserves proved their worth in the First and Second World Wars. They provided the base or platform from which large military forces could be raised in short periods of time. For instance, a military force in excess of 600,000 people was raised in World War I. Of late, military strategists have given the matter of reserve forces some study. In terms of nuclear war, the strategists thought for awhile that perhaps we no
October 23, 1981

longer needed reserves, that if a war took place, it would be fought with the people who were on the spot and already trained, with the equipment on hand. The idea was that the war would not last more than a few days. Subsequently they have changed their ideas on that. Now we see that reserve forces might well play a major role in a major conflict.
Aside from their potential uses in wartime, they can be used to support the regular forces in their peacetime duties. Now it is agreed by all strategists who have thought about this, that Canada needs a reserve force. It plays a vital role and should be properly maintained and supplied. Certainly this was our view when we were in government. Our plan was to equip and supply the reserve forces adequately.
I should like to make a brief mention of the cadets. There are some 60,000 cadets in Canada-air cadets, sea cadets and those attached to the army. In particular, I congratulate the people responsible for building up a cadet force in my part of the country, in Canada's north. There are few things that young people can do to be a part of Canada. The establishment of the cadets has had a very beneficial effect. It has taught young people useful things. It has given them a sense of citizenship. They have been given the opportunity to do something useful with their lives by joining the regular forces when they graduate from school, if they so wish. Even if they do not decide on a military career, they will have done a lot of good for themselves and, what is more important, they will have done something good for Canada.
I should also like to see the re-establishment of the Canadian officer training corps. This has been allowed to lapse, but I think it should be established again in Canadian universities; indeed, I have never understood why it was discontinued. Many of the comments I made about cadets could be repeated with regard to the officer training corps. I understand that there is certainly a critical shortage of young, trained, junior officers in the Canadian forces. We should look to the universities to train these people and, to that end, the officer training corps should be re-established.
I should like now to deal with the Canadian rangers. In my opinion, this was a very elite part of the reserve. It is about 1,000 strong and is peculiar to northern Canada. Reserve units exist in many small northern communities, some only five or ten men strong. These people have been chosen because of their special knowledge of the local area. Should we ever have to fight in the north-and I hope that will never be the case- these people could render invaluable assistance to regular forces fighting on terrain and under conditions totally unfamiliar to them.
In peacetime, the Canadian rangers could also fulfil a vital role. All kinds of things could go wrong in the north for which their services might be required. An incident which immediately comes to mind is the crash of the Russian satellite in my constituency not too long ago.
I am pleased at the way a number of distinguished officers commanding the northern region, such as Major General
National Defence
Thorneycroft, General Withers, Brigadier General Beattie, and Brigadier General Baile who is there at present, have gone out of their way to build up the cadet force and the ranger force. They have travelled from one small area to the other to give scattered ranger units the encouragement they need. In particular I should like to commend the Nanook ranger series of exercises which have been conducted in the last few years.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that although we have some slight reservation about the wording of the bill, we can certainly support the concept. We would encourage full support for a Canadian reserve force, and we hope that the subcommittee, which presently has this matter under study, will report favourably to the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should also like to offer my congratulations to the hon. member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) for bringing Bill C-359 to the attention of the House and calling for a reference to a subcommittee of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.
The hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) complained that the hon. member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore gave a 40-minute speech in 20 minutes. The usual complaint in this place is just the reverse; far too many of us make a 20-minute speech and take 40 minutes in which to do it. I congratulate the hon. member on the speediest presentation that I have heard in some time.
Even though we were not able to follow all his swiftly uttered words, I understand there is some disposition to have this matter go to the subcommittee, and therefore I shall not use up my 20 minutes. Perhaps half that time will take care of what I want to say this afternoon.
In a way, I am substituting for this party's defence critic who is a member of that committee, the hon. member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Sargeant). He had to leave for Manitoba in order to deal with a little electoral unpleasantness caused by Premier Sterling Lyon. If he were here, I am sure he could deal with many of the details of the bill. Even though a number of my constituents have spoken to me of their concern about the appalling state of the reserve unit in this country, I do not think it is possible for me to deal with every aspect of this matter, so, like the hon. member for Western Arctic, I shall make some general remarks.
I should like to outline my reservation about the reference to the subcommittee. I support the reference but I do so with some real reservations. It is common knowledge around the Hill that this subcommitee has not been very productive. As a matter of fact, this information has filtered beyond the Hill, and I shall refer to this in my remarks.
The House gave a reference to the standing committee to report on the status, capabilities and role of the Armed Forces late last winter, with instructions to report by December 15 next. It was not until March 24 that the reference for a subcommittee was passed by the standing committee. On May

October 23, 1981
National Defence
14, the subcommittee eventually met for the first time, and it was not until June 16 that it began to discuss how it would approach the subject. Yesterday it heard its first witness in public but, as it must report to the full committee by December 7, that will indicate to anyone with a slight knowledge of how subcommittees work, that it can only have about two and a half weeks left for hearings. There are still dozens of submissions to be heard on this very important subject. When the printing requirements, the time necessary for translation, the time necessary to get the committee to agree or disagree with subcommittee recommendations, are all taken into consideration, it is clear that the task is impossible. I am concerned about that, as are a number of other people.
I said that it is common knowledge on the Hill that the committee was not working well. This knowledge has spilled into the press, as is evidenced in the article by Douglas Fisher which appeared in today's Toronto Sun. I bring this up not to excoriate the subcommittee chairman but to point out that Parliament cannot ignore what is being broadcast in the media. I will quote that part of the article which shows that there is an urgent need to deal with the Armed Forces and the problems that relate to the reserve. The article reads in part as follows:
Unfortunately, this urgency has not affected the work of the subcommittee, chaired by a Liberal MP, Maurice Harquail. Two months passed before the chairman called an organization meeting. Another month passed before a second meeting in mid-June. Over the period of the summer recess the committee was briefed and cosseted by the regular force military commands across Canada. (The committee did not use this opportunity to meet with the reserve troops, sailors and airmen who may be affected by their report or who could profile all that's haywire in the current reserves. Instead, the committee will receive their written submissions and hold hearings in Ottawa under the benign gaze of the defence department mandarins. This leaves the impression the report will be an inside job-
Fisher closes this portion with a quote:
-whatever the Chief of Defence-
He does not say "wants". I think it is a typo that was left out; but I think that is the impression he was intending to leave. I am worried about this, and not just because of its subject matter. One of the things that we have noted here in this session of Parliament is the excellent work of task forces and subcommittees. We have had them on a lot of topics. We have had one on alternative energy of which I was a member, as was my colleague, the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. MacBain), chaired by the hon. member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle (Mr. Lefebvre). By all accounts, it was a thorough, capable-if not outstanding-job.
We have had the committee on the handicapped, chaired by the present parliamentary secretary to the House leader. We have had the North-South. They have all gotten down to work. They have done their homework, they have studied and they have reported. We know, from the length of time it has taken some of us and the hours we have put in on that work, how demanding a job it is, how complex it can be, and how long it takes. One cannot do it in two and a half weeks of public hearings if one is going to do a thorough job. It just cannot be
done. As a matter of fact, with his interest in this subject, I do not know why the subcommittee was not headed by the hon. member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson). Other Liberals have done thorough and favourable work as heads of these task forces and subcommittees, so 1 think that if he has that interest, perhaps he should have been the one.
I make reference to this because it is terribly disappointing, not just to parliamentarians, but also to the 19,000 or so Canadians who serve their country in the reserves. They do not do it for the money. They do not even get beer money out of it, really. They are doing it for a commitment; that is why they are doing it. I think they have a right to expect from Parliament much more than just a once over lightly kind of look at their problems. We will be letting them down unless we give an extension of the time permitted to the subcommittee and make some other arrangements. I see that the parliamentary secretary to the minister is here and I am pleased that she is. I know she must be concerned as well.
Dozens of other organizations and individuals have made submissions. They want to be heard. They have submitted briefs, they have indicated their willingness to appear before the committee, and they will not have a chance because the hearings are in Ottawa and there are only two and a half weeks left.
Let me turn to some of the other things more directly related to the bill. In principle, I support the bill before us. Perhaps the reservations about certain kinds of federal institutions mentioned by Northern Transportation Company Ltd. and by the hon. member for Western Arctic would have to be considered, but we are really referring the subject matter of the bill to the committee. Certainly, if one wanted, federally chartered companies could probably be added to the list of Crown corporations and other government agencies which might be included. However, the guidelines certainly have to be worked out. That is not our purpose here. Our purpose here is to deal not with the details, but with the principle of the reference.
If we are going to have a Canadian reserve, there must be proper training. The members have to get away sometime for training and vacations; maybe not two months, but two weeks at a minimum. They must have some training periods of reasonable length. More important, they ought to be able to train as units. This is now largely impossible because members of reserve forces, for the most part, can only train during their summer holidays and, of course, their vacations do not always coincide. That is another problem.
In addition, maybe we are asking too much of people who are already giving up one or two evenings a week and some weekends with their families in the service of their country; but, in addition to asking them to do two or three evenings a week or one or two evenings on weekends, we are now going to ask them to give up their summer holidays with their families, without any adequate kind of recompense at all. They probably will not receive the most effective training should some of the other conditions alluded to earlier take place.
October 23, 1981

I think this bill would overcome some of these problems and substantially contribute to the capability of the reserve forces. It would say, to each and every one of those people who are members of the reserves, that this country cares about what they are doing, and so does Parliament.
I would like to talk for a minute or two about the fact that there may be some debate about the role the reserves should play in Canada. We have reserves. There is no debate at all about the fact that they have been neglected, that their morale is down to zero, and that they suffer the inadequacies of poor equipment and inadequate training.
We are just about reaching Remembrance Day. We are not very far away from it. I guess my first memory of the reserves, then called the militia, goes back to the time when I was in elementary school. My elementary school principal was an officer in the Westminster regiment. We had cadets in the school at the time, and we had uniforms and all those things which probably would look out of place today. There were all kinds of other things and attitudes that we do not have today, too; but I will not go into those. When World War I was declared in 1939-

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE GROWTH OF RESERVE FORCE
MEASURE TO ENCOURAGE GROWTH OF RESERVE FORCE
speechtext:
-who were the first ones to march off? My high school principal and the members of the reserve who trained in what was then called the Mission Rink, which has now been torn down. We later called it the armouries, and there are all kinds of names it was called. However, the fact is that there was an active group, part of the New Westminster reserve unit, the New Westminster regiment, training there at all times. They were the first to respond to the call when the call came, when trouble came.
If we let the reserves run down, as we have been doing, then who will respond the next time trouble occurs? Some people say that it will not matter, anyway, because when they start throwing those A-bombs around at one another, it will not matter whether we have reserves; we might as well have a few guys out there with pointed sticks or big shovels to dig holes. I do not know. However, maybe having reserve units can do something to at least prevent the last resort being used. Again, we could get a lot of arguments, both within and outside my party on that one. I remember the cadets; I remember the New Westminsters. 1 remember how they responded in World War 1 and in Korea.
Almost every industrialized nation, both in the East and the West Bloc, has a ratio of three in the reserves to one in the regular forces. Our ratio is exactly the reverse. We have three in the regular forces for every one in the reserves. We are out of step or something. The Senate subcommittee on this subject suggested that in wartime we probably need 108,000 reserves. We have 30,000 on paper, and obviously that is a force, even if they could all serve, which would be too small to discharge its obligations. Besides, how many could go, out of those 30,000 that are on paper? Some would be too old, some would be too young, and some would not be suitable for
National Defence
certain kinds of combat roles, and therefore, it is a serious problem.
The hon. member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore talked about augmentation. The reserves will be used, as a policy, to augment the regular forces; but if they are not trained as units, how can they? How can they adequately augment a regular force unit if their training is individual? For instance, an example is the Winnipeg Rifles. They do not train as a formation; they train as individuals. They would never go into action as a formation or work together as a formation. People who are much more knowledgeable than I in this particular area say that this will have some alarming consequences.
If we are going to augment the regular forces with the reserve units, why do we not arm the reserve units with the same equipment that is being used by the regular forces? There are some armoured reserve units which have scarcely seen a tank in this country, with the exception, perhaps, of a Sherman tank, but certainly not the Leopard tanks which are being used over in Europe. Naval reserves, I am told, are still using four-inch guns, probably two weapons generations behind what modern naval units are using. There are probably other examples that, if you searched, you could probably find, very easily, but I do not think I need to do so in order to make the point.
We need strong support by the regulars if our reserve units are to be functional. They are doing the training, they are the professionals and the ones who will be up to date. I do not want anybody to mistake what I am saying. I do not want to malign anyone. However, it has frequently been the practice that the officers from the regular forces chosen to train the reserve units are people an inch away from retirement. I am not suggesting that some of them do not do an excellent job, and I said I did not want to malign anyone. However, I think the greater number of them used to train the reserve units should be ambitious young officers whose record in reserve training would somehow help them in their advancement. I would look for that. Again I am sure there are many officers who are about to be retired who do excellent work, but I think there should be a better balance between young and older or nearly retired officers training the reserves.
I suggest the committee should take a look at these things. Just because we are different from some countries in Europe and the United States in that we do not have conscription, as some countries do, does not mean we are all wrong, but it certainly will not hurt to look at this.
I am a little concerned that, while we do support this reference and request today, we cannot have all that much confidence that the committee, if it continues to perform as it has in the last six months, will accomplish much, or that much will happen with the reference. I am sorry to say that, but I think that needs to be said.

tunity to correct the record in at least two instances and add, with reference to the last statement by the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose), to say that in my view it is very sad indeed that the author of the article to which he referred was not even present yesterday. It is unfortunate he was not present, as I was, because he would have heard three of the best briefs I have personally heard in a long time. The committee is working.
Another reference in the same article which he quoted said that the subcommittee on reserves had not spoken to the ranks, only to officers. I can assure the hon. member and the author of that article, and I wish he would come to the meetings before he covers them in the press, that we did speak to the "other ranks", both at Gagetown and Petawawa. In fact, at Petawawa I personally had the great thrill of being able to drive in a tank, and I assure you it was not an officer who drove it.
The other point I want to correct, and I think this is important for the record, relates to the fact that the mover of this motion, echoed by our friend from across the way, the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), misquoted some figures. They both referred to the present paid strength of the reserves as being under 21,000, and said it has fallen this last year. I am happy to report-and again, if the author of that report had been at the meeting yesterday he would have known-that the present strength of the reserves as of June of this year, far from being 19,000, is 22,898. So much for inaccurate reporting.
There were many other points I would have enjoyed making on this very important matter, but as a sign that this particular government and the minister, whom I am proud to represent in the House this afternoon, are much more anxious for action
than for words, I will cut short my speech and move, seconded by the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Bossy):
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
"Bill C-359, an act to encourage the growth of the Reserve Force of the
Canadian Forces, be not now read a second time but that the order be
discharged, the bill withdrawn and the subject matter thereof referred to the
Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence."
